title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Ypsilanti pauses utility builds for a U-M data center; why towns across Michigan are hitting the brakes.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Today we're diving into why one Washtenaw County township just put the brakes on big electric projects that could feed new data centers.
Right, and it's not the only place pushing back this week.
Let's start with the big story out of Ypsilanti Township.
Graham, what exactly did the board do on Monday?
Trustees voted unanimously to approve a land-use moratorium aimed at major utility infrastructure that would support data centers.
And this directly hits a proposed project involving the University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory at Textile and Bridge roads?
That's the one. The pause limits new big power lines or substations that could serve heavy users like that research facility.
Why would a township go after the infrastructure instead of the data center itself?
It gives them time to study impacts on power demand, land use, and local resources before anything gets locked in.
That makes sense when you think about how fast these projects can move once utilities commit.
Exactly. We've seen similar pauses pop up in other counties this week too.
Like St. Joseph County weighing its own year-long moratorium after resident concerns about power and water.
And Forsyth Township up in the U.P. held a town hall where folks raised the same issues around noise and utility strain.
So what's the history here in Ypsilanti specifically?
The University of Michigan has been expanding its supercomputing needs, and this site was floated as a way to support that plus national lab research.
But locals are worried about what that means for everyday electric bills and water use.
Right. Data centers are massive power hogs, and Michigan's grid is already tight in places.
How does a project like this affect rates for regular households?
The bigger the demand spike, the more utilities may need to upgrade or buy extra power, which can get passed along.
We've heard that warning in Mason and Bay City too.
Yes, residents there packed meetings saying the projects could push local systems past capacity and raise costs.
What about water? These facilities need a lot for cooling, don't they?
They do, especially in areas where groundwater or municipal supplies are already stretched.
And farmland or open space gets turned into industrial sites.
That's the land-use angle the moratorium is trying to address before contracts are signed.
Who are the main players pushing for these projects?
Universities, national labs, and private developers looking for cheap land and available power.
And on the other side, township boards and residents worried about long-term costs versus promised tax revenue.
We've seen that debate in Gibraltar too, where a developer is now suing after the city rejected a project.
That lawsuit could set a precedent for how much local zoning power really holds up.
Exactly. Wayne County folks 30 miles away will be watching how that plays out.
What happens next in Ypsilanti after this moratorium?
Officials get time to write new rules on utility projects and assess the full impact on the grid and residents.
Meanwhile, the proposed U-M and Los Alamos site is on hold for now.
And this fits into a broader pattern we're seeing statewide.
Yesterday the Michigan Public Service Commission released energy cost recommendations, and advocates are calling for stronger data center protections.
That timing feels connected to all these local fights.
How might those recommendations help ratepayers?
They aim to lower overall energy costs while giving the commission more tools to review big loads like data centers.
Still, some want faster guardrails so communities aren't left footing the bill.
Detroit Free Press reporting from yesterday shows what daily life is like next to existing large facilities.
Constant hum, more traffic, and higher utility bills for neighbors.
That's the concrete side of the debate people 30 or 60 miles away might not see yet.
And one resident who tried to recall officials over a data center vote is now pushing rule changes after the effort failed.
It shows how these fights can spill into local politics and accountability questions.
So the Ypsilanti move is part of a wave, not an isolated case.
Right. Towns are using moratoriums to buy time while the state figures out bigger policy.
What should listeners watch for in the coming weeks?
How other counties respond, any new state rules on cost allocation, and whether projects get redesigned or relocated.
Now let's hit some of the other stories from today quickly.
Bay City neighbors packed a planning meeting to oppose proposed data centers over power, water, and noise concerns.
That outcry is showing up in more mid-Michigan towns as people question the rapid spread.
In Mason, city council heard warnings that a project would strain utilities and raise household rates.
Speakers wondered if tax revenue would really cover the long-term costs to residents.
St. Joseph County is considering its own year-long pause to write rules before projects lock in land and contracts.
Southwest Michigan communities will feel the ripple effects on how fast these spread into rural areas.
Gibraltar is facing a lawsuit after rejecting a data center, putting local zoning power to the test.
Wayne County residents will track how that shapes future fights near Detroit.
Up north, Forsyth Township residents pressed officials at a town hall on noise, power, and water from a Sawyer area proposal.
Marquette County taxpayers could see higher bills if it moves forward.
And Ypsilanti's moratorium also ties into halting big utility builds that could support U-M supercomputer expansion.
The pause lets officials assess power demand and land-use impacts first.
Now for what's on deck today.
Lodi Township has its Data Center Subcommittee meeting this evening to discuss ordinance and planning.
Somerset Township Board of Trustees meets too, and a proposed data center moratorium ordinance could come up.
Grass Lake Charter Township Planning Commission is also in session, with data center topics possibly on the agenda.
Listeners can check those if they want to weigh in locally.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Ypsilanti Moratorium Targets Data Center Power Lines as Pushback Spreads
